newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cabinet approves steel privatisation plan.
newsitem.headline: Czech cabinet approves steel privatisation plan.

text.p: The Czech government on Wednesday approved a plan to privatise stakes in two steelworks -- Nova Hut a.s. and Vitkovice a.s. -- which officials hailed as a novel way to encourage restructuring of an industry.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said the plan includes putting shares on the equity market and a phased-in management buy out, with incentives for restructuring, as the mills face stiffer competition from the European Union and rivals further east.
Under the plan the state would sell shares totalling 19 percent in both companies on the stock market while each company's management would get a one percent stake.
The mills' management would also get a five-year option to get a further 10 percent stake, which could only be executed if they succeed with their restructuring plans for the companies.

Details of the stock floatation were not yet available, but Klaus said it was expected to take place by the year's end. The state's shares in both Vitkovice and Nova Hut are held by the privatisation agency the National Property Fund.

"It is a relatively new approach to the privatisation of companies, and is a certain form of a manager contracts, making the management interested," Klaus told a news conference after a cabinet meeting.
"I think that this way (of privatisation) should be used in companies of this kind as well," he added.
Both steel mills are located in the northeast city of Ostrava.
The plan was drafted by Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy who has been searching for years for a way to ease the state out of the steel business and make the industry more efficient.

In drafting the plan, Dlouhy said his ministry concluded that the managements of both companies had well-defined their business plans, restructuring aims, and had a good analysis of sales opportunities.
He said criteria for the increased management stake included transparency of ownership, cooperation with local authorities, and increasing the firms' market value.
Penalties for failing to fulfil the restructuring commitments were also built into the deal.
Dlouhy said that if a 51 percent stake was sold, the majority owners could block dividend payments and use all profit for repayment of the loans they took for the stock purchase.
Under an earlier plan, both neighbouring firms would combine their pig iron production at Nova Hut.
The state holds just over 68 percent in both mills after some shares were privatised through the government's massive waves of selloffs in the early 1990s.
Dlouhy also said that after the year 2000 the state would start gradually selling off its remaining stakes.
